commands.name: status
commands.description:
Report every provider's credential: where it comes from and whether it works. Never prints values.

Without --check only presence is reported (status `unchecked` or `missing`).
Exits 0 when every required provider is ok/unchecked (an optional one may be
missing), 3 when any required provider has a problem or any credential is
invalid/expired, 2 on a usage error. A per-target provider (one credential per
site/host/account) gets one entry per stored target, named `<kind>:<target>`. The --json shape is a cross-tool contract:
`tool`, `version`, `checked_at`, `credentials[]` with `provider`, `required`,
`fields`, `source`, `source_ref`, `status`, `expires_at`, `quota`, `message`.

Example: semkit auth status --check --json

commands.name: read
commands.description:
Read a table, run the steps in the order written, write the result: one pipeline.

Each step works on the current table. A change step rewrites the working column
(with --as NAME it writes a new column), a filter keeps or drops rows, a report
(n-grams) makes its table the current one and its first text column the working one.
After each step one line goes to stderr: the step, the rows before and after it,
the cells it changed. Every step and option is checked before the input is read.

Every column is read as text; an empty cell is an empty string. An option that
takes items takes a comma list 'a,b', @FILE (one item per line) or @NAME of a list
(@stop/semtools, @minus/cheap…; `semkit lists` shows them all). `semkit read IN STEP --help` shows a step.

Example: semkit read core.csv remove-words --items купить dupes --kind lemmas --action drop write out.csv

options.name: --column
options.description: The working column the steps read and change; by default the first text column.

options.name: --whole
options.description: Read a text file as one cell of the column text (an article).

options.name: --trace
options.description: Write every cell a step changes and every row it drops to FILE as JSONL: row, step, column, before, after.

options.description: Read and run every step, print the summary, write nothing.

commands.name: ngrams
commands.description:
Every run of `n` words over all phrases, counted: a table ngram, count, docs, sum and forms.

count: occurrences. docs: in how many distinct index values (texts, when `sk.split_text` cut the phrases) the gram occurs at least once; the add-in has no such column, it is a semkit addition, so the conformance cases compare count and sum only. sum: with `weight`. forms: with `lemmas`, the word forms met for the gram, most frequent first, joined by ', ' («диваны, диван»); for a gram of several words its distinct spellings, at most 5.

Sorted by count, biggest first, then by ngram. Words are compared by case and ё.
lemmas: count lemmas of the words («диваны» is «диван»), by `lemmatizer`.
stopwords: False makes the runs of words that are no stopwords; a stopword between two of them stays inside the gram («купить диван в москве» gives «купить диван» and «диван в москве»), as «Биграмм без учета стоп-слов»; stopwords are found in any case (ADR 0005).
weight: a numeric column of the table; `sum` adds its value once per occurrence.

The step counts the working column; the table replaces the current one, its column ngram is the working one.

Example: semkit read core.csv ngrams write out.csv

options.description: See the description above.

options.name: --lemmas
options.description: count lemmas of the words («диваны» is «диван»), by `lemmatizer`.

options.name: --weight

The step counts the working column; the table replaces the current one, its column ngram is the working one.

Example: semkit read core.csv bigrams write out.csv

commands.name: counts
commands.description:
One count per phrase, as a Series or a new column `<column>_<what>`.

what: "words" and "chars" — the words and the characters of the phrase; "count" — how many times the same phrase stands in the core; "number" — which occurrence of it this row is (1 for the first). Phrases are the same by case and ё (ADR 0005); an empty cell has no count (empty value). "share" — the cumulative share of the sum of `weight` (0..1) in row order; "share_of_total" — the value over the sum; both are empty when the sum is 0. "abc" — the class by the cumulative share from the heaviest phrase down: "A" up to 80 %, "B" up to 95 %, "C" the rest. "share", "share_of_total" and "abc" need `weight`.

The step writes the count of each phrase to a new column <column>_count.

Example: semkit read core.csv counts купить write out.csv

commands.name: change-case
commands.description:
The phrase in another case, by `kind`:

- "lower", "upper": the whole phrase; - "title": every word capitalised, the rest lower; a letter after a digit or a sign starts a word too («иван-петров 5g» → «Иван-Петров 5G»); - "sentence", "sentence_lower": the first letter of the text and of each sentence (after «.», «!», «?» and spaces) upper or lower; the other letters stay; - "latin_title": a word that starts with a small latin letter gets it capital («iphone» → «Iphone»); - "latin_upper": a word with a latin letter in upper case whole («wi-fi-роутер» → «WI-FI-РОУТЕР»); - "list_title", "list_upper": the words of `words` capitalised or upper (case and ё do not count); - "toponyms": the place names of the bundled geo list as the list spells them («нижний новгород» → «Нижний Новгород»), the longest name from each word; - "abbreviations": a word of 2 to 5 consonants, or 3 to 5 vowels, upper («hp», «ооо»), then each word of the bundled abbreviations as the list spells it («спб» → «СПб», «usb» → «USB», «СМ» → «см»).

The word kinds split the phrase on any whitespace and join the words by one space.

The step rewrites the working column; with --as NAME it writes the result to a new column NAME.

Example: semkit read core.csv change-case купить write out.csv

commands.name: match-type
commands.description:
The phrase with the operators of a match type, by `kind`:

- "broad": «A в Б», every «+», «!», «[», «]» and «"» taken out; - "plus_every_word": «+A +в +Б»; "broad_modifier": «+A в +Б», the stopwords plain; - "stopword_modifier": «A +в Б», `modifier` ("+" or "!") on the stopwords only; - "fixed_forms": «!A !в !Б»; "quoted_fixed_forms": «"!A !в !Б"»; "quoted_fixed_order": «"[!A !в !Б]"»; - "brackets": «[A в Б]»; "quotes": «"A в Б"»; - the exact match is "quotes", "quoted_fixed_forms" and "quoted_fixed_order" for Yandex, "brackets" for Google; the phrase match is "brackets" for Yandex, "quotes" for Google; - "antisemantic": «[A] в [Б]», each word but the stopwords in brackets.

A word that has an operator keeps it, and no other is added; the minus-words keep their place, and the kinds that wrap the phrase put them after it («"купить диван" -бесплатно»). Stopwords are found in any case. An empty phrase stays empty; the words are joined by one space ("broad" keeps the spaces as they are).

The step rewrites the working column; with --as NAME it writes the result to a new column NAME.

Example: semkit read core.csv match-type купить write out.csv

commands.name: fix-word-order
commands.description:
The words of the phrase in the order of a search query: «диван для гостиной раскладной кожаный» → «кожаный раскладной диван для гостиной».

1. The complements go to the end: a preposition (для, с, без, в, из, на…) with the words after it up to the last noun among the next 5, stopping at the next preposition or at `main_word`. 2. The adjectives that agree with the main word in `form` go first: masculine («кожаный»), feminine («кожаная»), feminine_accusative («кожаную»), plural («кожаные»). 3. The words of the bundled list of words that start a query (где, купить, недорогой, кожаный…, in that form) go first, in the order of the list.

main_word: the object of the query, one word (case and ё do not count): a complement never takes it. complements=False: only step 3. The words are joined by one space.

The step rewrites the working column; with --as NAME it writes the result to a new column NAME.

commands.name: compare-grams
commands.description:
How the grams of my text differ from the competitors' texts: a row per gram met in any competitor.

mine: one text (a str). competitors: texts one per row (a Series, or a DataFrame with `column`). The density of a gram in a text is its count / the words of that text; a competitor without the gram counts as 0. Grams are those of sk.ngrams (`n`, `lemmas`, `stopwords`).
Columns: ngram. docs: competitors that hold it. docs_share: docs / competitors, 0..1. median, min, max: the density in the competitors. mine: its density in my text. verdict: 'below', 'within' or 'above', mine against median x (1 ± tolerance); when the median is 0, 'within' if mine is 0, else 'above'. Densities are rounded to 4 decimals. Sorted by median, biggest first, then ngram. The only norm is the median.

competitors: a file with the texts of the competitors, one per row, in its first text column; the file is read like `read` does.

The step takes the working column as my text (its cells, one per line); the table of the comparison replaces the current one.

commands.name: bm25
commands.description:
Okapi BM25 of each text for `query`: a Series of scores, rounded to 4 decimals, with the index of `texts`.

Terms are the lemmas without stopwords, on both sides; a term repeated in the query counts once. The length of a text is its number of terms. idf = ln((N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5) + 1); N, df and the average length are taken over the given texts, so to rank my text among the competitors pass all of them together. score = sum over the terms of idf x tf x (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1 x (1 - b + b x length / average length)). A text without a term of the query scores 0.

The step takes each cell of the working column as a text and writes its score for the query to a new column <column>_bm25; to rank my text among the competitors, put all the texts in the working column.

Example: semkit read core.csv bm25 купить write out.csv

commands.name: text-stats
commands.description:
The usual SEO metrics of each text, the same numbers each run: a table with the input index, a row per text.

A cell is a text; an empty cell (None, NaN, "") gives zeros and an empty `top`. With a DataFrame and `column=` the metric columns are added right after `column` to your table, which is returned.

Words: the punctuation of sk.chars('punctuation') is dropped (a hyphen between two word characters stays, «кресло-кровать» is one word), the rest splits on whitespace, case and ё are folded. Stopwords are the bundled list of the n-grams. Lemmas are the words that are no stopwords, by `lemmatizer`. A unit without a meaning (руб, рублей, шт, см, мм, мл, кг, кв, стр, ул) is a word but no lemma for top, nausea, ttr, mtld and zipf. Columns, in this order:
chars: all characters of the text. chars_no_spaces: the same without whitespace.
words: the words of the text, stopwords and units included.
unique: distinct lemmas of the words that are no stopwords (units included).
water: stopwords / words, 0..1.
nausea_classic: the square root of the count of the most frequent lemma (the top), 2 decimals.
nausea_academic: that count / words, 0..1.
top: that lemma; on a tie, the first in the text.
ttr: distinct lemmas / lemmas, 0..1 (lemmas as above: no stopwords, no units).
mtld: Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity (McCarthy and Jarvis 2010), threshold 0.72. Read the lemmas forward: each time the running type/token ratio falls to 0.72 or below, count a factor and restart; the last partial run adds (1 - ttr) / (1 - 0.72). Do it backward too; mtld = lemmas / mean of the two factor counts, 2 decimals; 0 for under 2 lemmas.
zipf: R² x 100, 1 decimal, of the linear regression of log count on log rank over the lemma counts (rank 1 is the biggest count), so f(r) = C / r^s fits; 0 for under 5 distinct lemmas. No norms and no verdicts: the caller sets them.

The step reads the working column; the metric columns are added right after it in the current table.

Example: semkit read core.csv text-stats write out.csv
